facts.title: Predicted Before Discovered
facts.text: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table and predicted an unknown element he called "eka-silicon," estimating its atomic weight, density, and oxide formula. When Clemens Winkler isolated germanium in 1886, its measured properties matched the prediction almost exactly. This stunning success became one of the strongest early confirmations that the periodic law was real.

facts.title: Named For Germany
facts.text: Clemens Winkler discovered the element in 1886 in Freiberg, Saxony, while analyzing a silver mineral called argyrodite. He named it after his home country, Germany (Latin Germania). For a brief moment he considered the name "neptunium," but that label was eventually given to a different element decades later.

facts.title: A Metal That Isn't
facts.text: Germanium is a metalloid: it looks like a shiny, silvery-white metal but behaves chemically and electrically like a semiconductor. At room temperature it is a brittle, crystalline solid that shares the same diamond cubic structure as silicon and carbon. This in-between nature is exactly why it became so important to electronics.

facts.title: It Powered The First Transistor
facts.text: The very first working transistor, built at Bell Labs in December 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley, was made from germanium, not silicon. Germanium dominated early electronics through the 1950s before silicon took over because it handles heat better and forms a more stable oxide. That single germanium device launched the entire age of modern computing.

facts.title: It Expands When It Freezes
facts.text: Like water and silicon, germanium is one of the rare substances that expands when it solidifies rather than contracting. Its liquid form is actually denser than its solid form, so solid germanium floats on its own melt. This anomaly comes from the open, tetrahedral crystal structure it forms when it freezes.

facts.title: Eyes For Night Vision
facts.text: Germanium is remarkably transparent to infrared light while being opaque to visible light, which makes it ideal for lenses and windows in thermal-imaging and night-vision cameras. Much of the world's germanium is used to make optics for military, firefighting, and security infrared systems. A polished germanium lens looks like dark metal to your eye but is crystal-clear to a heat camera.

facts.title: The Backbone Of Fiber Optics
facts.text: Adding germanium dioxide to the silica core of an optical fiber raises its refractive index, allowing light to be guided down the fiber over long distances. This doping is essential to the high-speed fiber-optic cables that carry most of the internet's data. A huge share of global germanium production goes into telecommunications glass.

facts.title: Hiding In Coal And Zinc
facts.text: Germanium is fairly rare, making up only about 1.6 parts per million of Earth's crust, and it has no rich ore of its own. Instead it is recovered mostly as a byproduct of zinc smelting and from the ash of certain coal deposits. China produces the majority of the world's supply, which makes germanium a strategically important critical mineral.

facts.title: Not Needed By Life
facts.text: Germanium has no known biological role in humans, plants, or animals, and the body does not require it. Despite this, some "organic germanium" supplements were marketed as health remedies, but inorganic germanium compounds taken over time have caused serious kidney damage and even deaths. Health agencies now warn against germanium dietary supplements.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Germanium is produced in the cosmos mainly through the slow neutron-capture process (the s-process) inside aging red giant stars, and partly in the explosive r-process of supernovae and neutron-star mergers. The germanium on Earth was inherited from such stellar debris that seeded the cloud which formed our solar system. Ultra-pure germanium crystals are even used today as detectors to hunt for gamma rays and dark matter.
